statement: Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.
heath_proof: For let as many numbers as we please, B, C, D, have been continually doubled beginning from the dyad A; I say that B, C, D are eventimes even only. Now that each of the numbers B, C, D is even-times even is manifest; for it is doubled from a dyad. I say that it is also even-times even only. For let an unit be set out. Since then as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit are in continued proportion, and the number A after the unit is prime, therefore D, the greatest of the numbers A, B, C, D, will not be measured by any other number except A, B, C. [IX. 13] And each of the numbers A, B, C is even; therefore D is even-times even only. [VII. Def. 8] Similarly we can prove that each of the numbers B, C is even-times even only.
ai_proof_text:
9.32
**Statement:** Each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only.

**Step 1.** Let the numbers A, B, C, D, ... be continually doubled beginning from a dyad. That is, consider the sequence of numbers in continued proportion beginning from the unit 1, with common ratio 2: namely 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. The numbers continually doubled beginning from a dyad are 2, 4, 8, 16, ..., being all terms of this sequence after the unit.

**Step 2.** We must show that each of these numbers is even-times even only, that is, each is even-times even (D7.8) but not even-times odd (D7.9).

**Step 3.** First, each number in the sequence is even. For each number after the first is produced by doubling the previous one, so each equals 2 times some number, and hence is divisible into two equal parts. By D7.6, each is even.

**Step 4.** Next we show each is even-times even. Consider any number in the sequence beyond the dyad itself, say C = 4, D = 8, and so on. Each such number is the product of two numbers both belonging to the sequence (for example, 4 = 2 times 2, 8 = 2 times 4, 16 = 2 times 8 or 4 times 4). Since every number in the sequence is even (Step 3), each such number is measured by an even number according to an even number. By D7.8, each is even-times even. The dyad 2 itself is also even-times even, since by D7.8 it is measured by 2 (an even number) according to 1 (the unit), and in the sequence from the unit, 2 is the product of the unit and an even number.

**Step 5.** It remains to show that none of these numbers is even-times odd. Suppose for contradiction that some number in the sequence, say N, is even-times odd. Then by D7.9, N is measured by an even number according to an odd number. This means there exists an odd number greater than 1 that measures N.

**Step 6.** Now the sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... consists of numbers in continued proportion beginning from the unit, and the number after the unit is 2, which is prime (D7.11, since 2 is measured by the unit alone among numbers). By Proposition 9.13, since the numbers are in continued proportion from the unit and the number after the unit (namely 2) is prime, no number in the sequence is measured by any number except those which have a place among the proportional numbers themselves.

**Step 7.** The numbers which have a place among the proportional numbers are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and so on. The unit 1 is not a number in the sense required for measurement by an odd number greater than 1. Every other term in the sequence is even, as shown in Step 3. Therefore no odd number greater than 1 measures any number in the sequence.

**Step 8.** This contradicts the supposition in Step 5 that an odd number greater than 1 measures N. Therefore N is not even-times odd.

**Step 9.** Since each number in the sequence is even-times even (Step 4) and not even-times odd (Step 8), each of the numbers which are continually doubled beginning from a dyad is even-times even only. Q.E.D.
